claim: get_nsec is a Tauri command with no access control that returns the raw bech32-encoded secret key to any caller from the renderer/JS context.
failure_scenario: Any XSS'd webview content, a malicious dependency loaded into the frontend bundle, or a compromised renderer process can call invoke('get_nsec') and immediately obtain the user's full private key in plaintext, with no confirmation dialog, rate limit, or additional authentication required from Rust's side.

votes.reasoning: The finding presupposes its own entry point ("any XSS'd webview content") without showing one. The desktop webview loads only the first-party bundled dist (desktop/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json frontendDist "../dist"); there is no WebviewUrl::External, no WebviewWindowBuilder for remote content, no <iframe> anywhere in desktop/src, and the only HTML sink is a locally generated identicon SVG (desktop/src/features/messages/ui/BotIdenticon.tsx:31). No attacker-controlled input reaches the renderer as script. Second, get_nsec is deliberate product functionality, not an oversight: the onboarding backup and profile reveal flows call it through desktop/src/shared/api/tauriIdentity.ts:29 and are covered by desktop/tests/e2e/onboarding-backup.spec.ts and profile-nsec-reveal.spec.ts. It also already goes through state.signing_keys() (identity.rs:192), so it is refused in recovery mode (app_state.rs:306-317). Third, the marginal gain is small: a renderer that can call invoke() at all already has sign_event (identity.rs:108, arbitrary event signing under the user's key), nip44_decrypt_from_self (identity.rs:684), create_ncryptsec_backup (identity.rs:243) and start_pairing (pairing.rs:73), i.e. full use of the identity. Any "confirmation dialog" would be rendered by the same renderer the scenario assumes is compromised. This is a design note about a feature every Nostr client ships, not a reachable vulnerability.

The quoted code is accurate but the finding is not a distinct vulnerability, and it misses two things. (1) get_nsec is NOT ungated: it calls state.signing_keys() (desktop/src-tauri/src/app_state.rs:306-322), which returns Err whenever identity_lost or keyring_locked is set, so it is subject to the same gate as every other signing command. (2) The claimed impact is not incremental. The same renderer, in the same trust position, can already reach commands registered in the same invoke_handler (desktop/src-tauri/src/lib.rs:686) that yield equivalent or total compromise: sign_event (identity.rs:108-136) signs arbitrary kinds/content with the user's key; create_ncryptsec_backup (identity.rs:242-254) takes an attacker-chosen password and returns a full NIP-49 encrypted key blob that the attacker can then decrypt offline; start_pairing (commands/pairing.rs:90-122) builds a payload literally containing the nsec. Removing or re-authing get_nsec would not close the exfiltration path, so 'renderer compromise -> key theft' is a property of the app's trust boundary, not of this function. Finally, the finding asserts XSS/renderer compromise as its premise without demonstrating any injection path: the only dangerouslySetInnerHTML in the desktop frontend is BotIdenticon.tsx:31 rendering a locally generated identicon SVG, and the webview loads bundled local content (tauri.conf.json frontendDist ../dist). get_nsec has legitimate first-party callers (BackupStep.tsx:117/143, PrivateKeyBackupRow.tsx:93, SignOutSection.tsx:84 — the show-your-nsec backup and sign-out flows). At most this is a defense-in-depth hardening suggestion (OS-level re-auth before revealing the key), not a critical finding.

The code reads as quoted (identity.rs:191-196) and the command is registered in the invoke handler (desktop/src-tauri/src/lib.rs:686), so a renderer can call it. But the claimed entry point — 'XSS'd webview content / malicious frontend dependency / compromised renderer' — is not an attacker entry point that gains anything: the same generated handler list registers create_ncryptsec_backup (lib.rs:689) and generate_backup_passphrase (lib.rs:688), and create_backup_with_log_n (identity.rs:214-234) will encrypt the live secret key under any password the caller supplies, returning the ncryptsec1 blob to the same renderer. import_identity (lib.rs:691) lets that same caller replace the key outright, and sign_event/create_auth_event let it sign arbitrarily. So any code that can invoke('get_nsec') can already extract the private key by invoking create_ncryptsec_backup('attacker-chosen-passphrase') and decrypting offline. get_nsec confers no privilege the postulated attacker does not already hold, and no remote party can reach it — the webview loads only the bundled local frontend (tauri.conf.json build.frontendDist '../dist'), and the single capability (capabilities/default.json, windows: ['main']) exposes no remote-content or arbitrary-URL webview. get_nsec is the backing command for the deliberate profile nsec-reveal feature (desktop/src/shared/api/tauriIdentity.ts:29, tests/e2e/profile-nsec-reveal.spec.ts). This is the app's trust model for a local key-holding client, not a reachable escalation.

claim: confirm_pairing_sas is a Tauri command that unconditionally proceeds to send the pending payload (which embeds the user's nsec, built in start_pairing) once called — there is no server-side (Rust) verification that the SAS codes actually matched; the 'confirmation' is purely the renderer calling this function.
failure_scenario: A compromised renderer script calls start_pairing() (returning the QR/session URI, which encodes the pairing session so a remote attacker can act as the pairing peer over the relay) and then immediately calls confirm_pairing_sas() without any human visually comparing SAS codes. Because the SAS check is a UI-only human decision never re-validated in Rust, the payload (JSON containing the raw nsec, see line 111-115) is sent over the pairing relay session to whatever peer completed the offer/SAS steps — letting a remote attacker who scripted the peer side of the protocol exfiltrate the full identity secret key with only renderer-JS execution, no physical device access or user interaction.
evidence:
pub async fn confirm_pairing_sas(pairing: State<'_, PairingHandle>) -> Result<(), String> {
    let tx = pairing
        .outbound_tx
        .lock()
        .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?
        .clone()
        .ok_or("no active pairing session")?;

votes.reasoning: Two independent reasons. (1) The premise is not a defect: a short authentication string is by construction an out-of-band human comparison. Rust cannot "re-validate" whether a human's eyes matched two numbers; the confirmation signal has to come from the UI layer in any SAS design. Calling that a missing server-side check is a category error. (2) The scenario grants the attacker nothing new. It starts from "a compromised renderer script calls start_pairing()" — but that same renderer can call invoke('get_nsec') (identity.rs:190) and receive the bech32 secret key in one step, or sign arbitrarily with sign_event (identity.rs:108). The pairing route is strictly harder (needs the QR relayed to a scripted peer, needs the peer to complete the offer/answer handshake at pairing.rs:73-140, needs the relay reachable) for an identical outcome. Note also the payload is only assembled after signing_keys() succeeds (pairing.rs:88) and is held in Zeroizing (pairing.rs:44, :121), and the qr_uri is displayed on-screen — a remote attacker without renderer code execution never obtains it. No escalation, no new capability.

The finding misreads what confirm_pairing_sas does and what SAS is. (1) Rust does enforce the protocol state machine, not nothing: PairingSession::confirm_sas (crates/buzz-core/src/pairing/session.rs:200-224) calls check_expired, expect_state(SessionState::Confirming) and expect_role(Role::Source), and errors out otherwise; Confirming is only ever entered by handle_offer (session.rs:184-191). send_payload repeats the state/role check (session.rs:232-234). So calling confirm_pairing_sas without a completed offer just returns an Err. (2) The 'remote attacker who scripted the peer side' cannot become the peer. handle_offer requires the offer to carry a session_id that constant-time-matches the source's derivation from the 32-byte random session_secret (session.rs:113-118 for generation, session.rs:168-175 ct_eq check), and that secret exists only inside the QR payload; the payload is then NIP-44 encrypted to the peer pubkey locked in at session.rs:178. Without the QR there is no session and no decryptable payload. (3) The premise is again a compromised renderer, which by the finding's own F001 already has invoke('get_nsec') — so there is no incremental capability here. (4) 'No server-side verification that the SAS codes matched' is definitionally true of every SAS/short-authentication-string protocol: the comparison is a human out-of-band check between two screens; software on either endpoint cannot re-verify a human's eyes. The target side likewise requires an explicit human approval (SessionState::AwaitingConfirmation / confirm_target_sas, session.rs:64-67). Also note start_pairing goes through state.signing_keys() (commands/pairing.rs:90), so the recovery-mode gate applies. No reachable failure distinct from 'the renderer is trusted'.

The claim that confirm_pairing_sas 'unconditionally proceeds' is wrong. The Rust side is state-machine gated: pairing.rs:161-166 calls PairingSession::confirm_sas, which enforces check_expired, expect_state(SessionState::Confirming) and expect_role(Role::Source) and requires both sas_input and a peer_pubkey to be present (crates/buzz-core/src/pairing/session.rs:200-208) before it will emit anything; send_payload independently requires SessionState::Transferring (session.rs:232-234). Calling start_pairing then confirm_pairing_sas back-to-back, as the failure scenario describes, returns an error — the session is not in Confirming until a remote peer has actually completed the offer/key-agreement round. A SAS comparison is by construction a human out-of-band check; there is nothing Rust could re-verify, since the code the user reads on the other device never enters this process. And the residual scenario still presupposes renderer code execution, which as with F001 already yields the key directly through get_nsec (lib.rs:686) or create_ncryptsec_backup (lib.rs:689) without any pairing peer, relay round-trip, or timing window. No privilege is gained.

claim: The NIP-09 ownership check in `parse_deletion_coordinate` (L219: `if owner != event.pubkey.to_hex() { return None; }`) is self-referential and therefore vacuous: it only requires the coordinate to name its own signer as owner. The subsequent local-store removals key on the attacker-chosen d-tag alone and never compare the record's owner, so a validly signed kind:5 from ANY keypair deletes the local persona / team / managed-agent record whose d-tag matches. The comment at L216-218 claims this check 'closes the other half — a validly signed kind:5 naming ANOTHER owner's coordinate must no-op', which the code does not achieve.
failure_scenario: Attacker generates keypair A and signs a kind:5 event whose `a` tag is `30177:<A_pubkey_hex>:<victim_agent_pubkey_hex>`. The owner segment equals the signer, so L219 passes and `parse_deletion_coordinate` returns `(30177, victim_agent_pubkey)`. `event.verify()` at L194-196 passes because the event is genuinely signed by A. Reaching `reconcile_inbound_tombstone`, L302-305 executes `agents.retain(|record| record.pubkey != target_d_tag)`, deleting the victim's ManagedAgentRecord — which is where `private_key_nsec` and `auth_tag` live — and `save_managed_agents` commits it without the keyring cleanup that `agents.rs:1334` performs on the normal delete path, orphaning the keyring entry. The same shape with `30175:<A>:<victim_persona_d_tag>` (L292-296) or `30176:<A>:<victim_team_id>` (L297-301) destroys personas and teams. Reachable today from a compromised/XSS'd renderer invoking `reconcile_inbound_persona_event` directly; the relay-delivered path is currently blocked by the TS-only `authors:[pubkey]` filter in usePersonaSync.ts:39, which inbound.rs:187-189 itself declares to be 'no defense'.
reported_slice: tauri-commands (buzz/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands) — Lens B: cryptography, keys, identity

votes.reasoning: The owner-equals-signer check really is logically weak, but the failure it enables is not reachable by any remote party. `reconcile_inbound_persona_event` is a Tauri command with exactly one production caller: `desktop/src/shared/api/tauriPersonas.ts:318` -> `desktop/src/features/agents/lib/usePersonaSync.ts:40`, and every event first passes `if (event.pubkey !== pubkey) return;` at usePersonaSync.ts:39, where `pubkey` is the local identity's own pubkey (AppShell.tsx:171 passes `identityQuery.data?.pubkey`). Both the live subscription (usePersonaSync.ts:60) and the one-shot backfill (usePersonaSync.ts:48) use `authors:[pubkey]` AND that explicit equality check. On the Rust side `parse_verified_inbound_event` (inbound.rs:190-198) calls `event.verify()`, so `event.pubkey` is the true signer. The two gates compose: an event only reaches `reconcile_inbound_tombstone` if it is genuinely signed by the user's own key. The attacker's fresh keypair A never survives usePersonaSync.ts:39 -- the field the reporter says is attacker-controlled is exactly the field being compared to the local identity, and the Rust signature check makes forging it impossible. The reporter's own fallback path ("compromised/XSS'd renderer invoking the command directly") is not a privilege gain: a renderer that can invoke arbitrary Tauri commands can already call the normal delete commands (agents.rs:1334 path) and every other persona/agent command registered at lib.rs:843. The inbound.rs:187-189 comment the reporter quotes says the TS owner filter is no defense *against a forged pubkey*, which is why the Rust verify() exists -- it does not say the filter is absent. Remaining value is defense-in-depth hardening only (comparing the record's stored owner before removal), with no reachable exploit in a shipped build.

The vacuousness of the owner check is real as written (inbound.rs:219 compares the coordinate owner to the event's own signer), but there is no attacker-reachable path to it. The one production caller of the Tauri command is the closure at desktop/src/features/agents/lib/usePersonaSync.ts:38-45, which begins `if (event.pubkey !== pubkey) return;` — where `pubkey` is the local user's own key. Both the live subscription (usePersonaSync.ts:60-64) and the one-shot backfill (usePersonaSync.ts:49-53) funnel through that same closure, so a relay (even a fully malicious one that ignores the `authors` filter) cannot get an event with a foreign pubkey past line 39. An attacker who instead sets the JSON `pubkey` field to the victim's key to pass line 39 is then killed by `event.verify()` at inbound.rs:194-196, since they cannot produce a Schnorr signature under the victim's key. The two checks compose: only events genuinely signed by the local identity reach `reconcile_inbound_tombstone`. The reporter's own admitted entry point — a compromised/XSS'd renderer — is not an escalation: a renderer that can call `invoke` can call the ordinary delete commands directly, which do more, not less. The comment at inbound.rs:187-189 ("the TS-side owner filter ... is no defense") is about the forged-pubkey case specifically and is correct about that case; it does not mean the filter is inert against foreign-authored events. Adding an `event.pubkey == our identity` assertion in Rust is worthwhile defense-in-depth, but no attacker input yields the described persona/team/managed-agent deletion in a shipped build.

The reporter missed an explicit client-side owner check and mischaracterised it as "the relay filter". desktop/src/features/agents/lib/usePersonaSync.ts:38-45 defines the only production reconcile callback as `const reconcile = (event: RelayEvent) => { if (event.pubkey !== pubkey) return; void reconcileInboundPersonaEvent(...) }`. That guard is client code, not a relay-side filter, so a hostile or non-compliant relay ignoring `authors:[pubkey]` still cannot get a foreign-authored event into the Tauri command: both the one-shot backfill (line 53) and the live subscription (line 63) funnel through the same `reconcile`, and `pubkey` is the local identity (`identityQuery.data?.pubkey`, AppShell.tsx:171-174). Combined with the coordinate-owner check at inbound.rs:219 (`owner == event.pubkey`), the shipped flow does enforce full NIP-09 scoping: coordinate owner == signer == local user. I also checked there is no second consumer — `KIND_DELETION` appears nowhere else in desktop/src-tauri/src (only inbound.rs:80/95/247/276), `reconcile_inbound_persona_event` has exactly one production caller (tauriPersonas.ts:322, wrapped by usePersonaSync; e2eBridge.ts is test-only), and neither `retain_inbound_event` nor `arrival_retention_scope` (retention.rs:98-107) rejects foreign pubkeys, so the TS guard is the enforcing hop. The only path the reporter can offer — "a compromised/XSS'd renderer invoking the command directly" — is an attacker who already has arbitrary Tauri-command execution and could simply call the normal delete command; that is not an escalation. Residual (hardening, not the claimed vulnerability): the Rust command does not itself compare `event.pubkey` against `state.signing_keys()`, so the owner rule lives in one language only, and the L215-218 comment overstates what L219 alone achieves.

claim: A live subscription's reconnect watermark `lastSeenCreatedAt` is set from the raw, unvalidated `created_at` of every inbound relay EVENT, so one event with a far-future timestamp permanently poisons the watermark and every subsequent reconnect replays with a `since` in the future — silently dropping all missed messages for that subscription for the rest of the session.
failure_scenario: Attacker path: (1) any community member (or the relay itself) publishes a kind:9/kind:11 event into channel X with `created_at = 4102444800` (year 2100). The relay's ingest path does not bound future timestamps — crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/command_executor.rs:121-125 only rejects timestamps that `chrono::DateTime::from_timestamp` cannot represent — so the event is stored and fanned out. (2) The victim's client receives it: relayClientSession.ts:783 matches the `EVENT` frame and calls `this.handleEvent(rest[0], rest[1] as RelayEvent)` with zero shape or range validation. (3) relayClientSession.ts:859 calls `prepareSubscriptionEvent(subscription, event)`. (4) relayClosedRecovery.ts:141-144 executes `subscription.lastSeenCreatedAt = Math.max(lastSeenCreatedAt ?? 0, event.created_at)` → the watermark becomes 4102444800 and can never be lowered (Math.max). (5) On the next socket drop, relayClientSession.ts:934 calls `replayLiveSubscriptions`, which at relayReconnectReplay.ts:170-176 computes `replaySince = max(0, 4102444800 - 5)` and at relayReconnectReplay.ts:61 builds the REQ filter with `since: Math.max(filter.since, since)`. (6) The REQ sent at relayReconnectReplay.ts:213-219 asks the relay for events newer than the year 2100, so the relay returns nothing. The victim's channel silently stops backfilling on every reconnect from then on — no error, no UI indication, and the paged-replay branch (`replayReconnectHistoryPages`, since > until) exits immediately too. One attacker message permanently breaks reconnect recovery for every client subscribed to that channel.

This is the single shared entry for BOTH transports: the WebSocket EVENT door (handlers/event.rs:728) and the HTTP bridge (api/bridge.rs:837) both call `ingest_event` (ingest.rs:1746), which wraps `ingest_event_inner`. Nothing between the top of `ingest_event_inner` (L1806) and the drift check returns successfully -- the only earlier returns are rejections (AUTH kind, membership notifications, HTTP-only gift wrap, relay-only kinds). Agent observer frames get an even tighter +/-300s window at handlers/event.rs:972-981. The `chrono::DateTime::from_timestamp` check the reporter quotes at command_executor.rs:121-125 is a later persistence step for command kinds, not the validation gate, so its permissiveness proves nothing. A kind:9/kind:11 with created_at = 4102444800 is therefore rejected at ingest and never stored or fanned out, so it never reaches relayClientSession.ts:783 or relayClosedRecovery.ts:141. The residual is a <=15-minute forward skew of `lastSeenCreatedAt` (also achievable by an honest client with a skewed clock), which self-heals as wall-clock passes the watermark -- not the claimed permanent, session-long poisoning. Bounding the client-side watermark by `Date.now()` is still reasonable hardening, but the finding as written does not hold.

The central premise is false. The relay bounds future timestamps for every ingested event: crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs:1859-1866 rejects any event whose created_at differs from server time by more than MAX_TIMESTAMP_DRIFT_SECS = 900 (±15 minutes). That check lives in `ingest_event_inner`, the single funnel behind `ingest_event` (ingest.rs:1746-1805), reached by both doors: the WebSocket EVENT frame at handlers/event.rs:728 and the HTTP bridge at api/bridge.rs:837. The line the reporter cites (command_executor.rs:121-125) is downstream of that gate, so its lenient `DateTime::from_timestamp` check is not the only bound. A kind:9/kind:11 with created_at = 4102444800 is rejected and never stored or fanned out, so the watermark cannot be set to the year 2100 and the claimed permanent poisoning cannot occur. The residual is bounded and self-healing: at most `now+900`, which stops mattering once wall-clock passes it — a ~15-minute backfill hole that closes by itself. Additionally, for exactly the channel subscriptions targeted, the reconnect REQ is sent with the unmodified filter, not the poisoned `since` (relayReconnectReplay.ts:212-218: `shouldPageReplay ? subscription.filter : buildReconnectReplayFilter(...)`), so the live re-subscribe still returns recent channel events; only the deep paged backfill is skipped.

The premise is factually wrong. The reporter cited command_executor.rs:121-125 (the persistence helper, which only guards `chrono::DateTime::from_timestamp` overflow) and concluded "the relay's ingest path does not bound future timestamps". The universal ingest path does bound them: crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs:1859-1866 in `ingest_event_inner` runs `const MAX_TIMESTAMP_DRIFT_SECS: i64 = 900; if (event_ts - now).abs() > MAX_TIMESTAMP_DRIFT_SECS { return Err(IngestError::Rejected("invalid: event timestamp too far from server time")) }` for every kind, immediately after signature verification and before any storage or fan-out. Both doors reach it — WebSocket via handlers/event.rs:728 and the HTTP bridge via api/bridge.rs:837, the only two callers of `ingest_event` (ingest.rs:1746). So step (1) of the scenario fails: a kind:9/11 with `created_at = 4102444800` is rejected, never stored, never fanned out, and the watermark at relayClosedRecovery.ts:141 never sees it. The residual is bounded and self-healing rather than permanent: a member can legitimately push the watermark at most ~15 minutes ahead, so a reconnect inside that window misses backfill until wall-clock catches up, and `lastSeenCreatedAt` lives on an in-memory subscription object that dies with the session anyway. A defensive clamp in `prepareSubscriptionEvent` would still be reasonable hardening against a hostile relay, but a hostile relay can withhold events outright, so it buys nothing against the stated adversary.

claim: queryEvents() pushes every relay-supplied EVENT payload straight into the results array and returns it to callers with no signature or id verification anywhere in the module (or anywhere else in the web slice — grep for verifyEvent/verifySignature found zero matches).
failure_scenario: A malicious or compromised relay (or a MITM on the WebSocket, or any code path that can inject EVENT frames) can send an event with an arbitrary `pubkey` field and fabricated `id`/`sig` that is never checked. Every consumer (use-repos.ts eventToRepo(), use-repo-refs.ts parseRefs()) trusts `event.pubkey` as the content's signer/owner and renders it as-is (PubkeyAvatar, repo owner/contributor lists), so an attacker-controlled relay can impersonate any pubkey to the browser client with no cryptographic contradiction ever surfacing to the user.

votes.reasoning: The code observation is accurate (queryEvents pushes relay payloads unverified at web/src/shared/lib/nostr-client.ts:135, and no verifyEvent exists in the web slice), but the claimed attacker cannot reach it. `queryEvents` is only ever called with `relayWsUrl()` — the two call sites are web/src/features/repos/use-repos.ts:66 and use-repo-refs.ts:55 — and `relayWsUrl()` (web/src/shared/lib/relay-url.ts:13-18) returns either the build-time `VITE_RELAY_URL` or a same-origin URL derived from `window.location`. There is no user-supplied relay input, no NIP-65 relay-list following, and `new WebSocket` appears nowhere else in web/src. So the only party that can inject EVENT frames is the origin that already serves the application bundle: it can rewrite the rendered page directly and gains nothing from forging a pubkey. The MITM variant is excluded by TLS on the wss:// URL derived from an https:// page (relay-url.ts:16). Client-side signature verification is worthwhile defense-in-depth for a future multi-relay client, but as shipped this is not reachable by an unprivileged attacker.

The only relay the web slice ever talks to comes from web/src/shared/lib/relay-url.ts:13-19 relayWsUrl(), which returns VITE_RELAY_URL if set and otherwise `${proto}//${window.location.host}`, i.e. the same origin that served the page; Justfile:576 sets VITE_RELAY_URL="${BUZZ_RELAY_URL}", the same deployment's relay. And on the honest-relay path the events are already signature-verified server-side before storage: crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/ingest.rs:1844 runs verify_event (buzz_core::verification::verify_event, imported at ingest.rs:39) in spawn_blocking and rejects on failure. Adding client-side verification would be reasonable defense-in-depth for a general-purpose Nostr client, but as shipped there is no attacker who gains anything, so this is not a high-severity auth-verification gap.

claim: `reconcile_inbound_persona_event` verifies the inbound event's Schnorr signature but never checks that `event.pubkey` equals the local owner's pubkey. `apply_inbound_persona` then matches purely on the `d`-tag and overwrites `system_prompt`, `model`, `provider`, and `respond_to_allowlist` on the local persona. Any validly-signed kind:30175 from ANY author whose d-tag collides with a local persona's d-tag rewrites that persona on disk. The only owner check in the whole flow lives in TypeScript (`usePersonaSync.ts:39` — `if (event.pubkey !== pubkey) return;`), which the Rust file's own doc comment at line 188 dismisses as "no defense", yet no Rust-side equivalent was added.

votes.reasoning: The crash premise is an unverified claim about Flutter engine internals, and it is wrong for the engine this app builds against (Dart SDK ^3.11.4, mobile/pubspec.yaml:6-7). A MethodChannel reply does not go through an @UiThread entry point: MethodChannel.IncomingMethodCallHandler.Reply forwards to DartMessenger.Reply, which calls FlutterJNI.invokePlatformMessageResponseCallback / invokePlatformMessageEmptyResponseCallback — these are the 'called on any thread' variants guarded by a `synchronized (this)` + isAttached() check, not by ensureRunningOnMainThread(). The @UiThread contract the reporter cites applies to the outbound direction (MethodChannel.invokeMethod / setMethodCallHandler / FlutterJNI.dispatchPlatformMessage), which is what Flutter's 'Jumping to the UI thread in Android' doc section is about. Decisive structural evidence: BinaryMessenger.TaskQueue (makeBackgroundTaskQueue) intentionally runs method-call handlers off the platform thread and replies through the exact same DartMessenger.Reply object; if replying off-thread threw, that supported feature could not exist. Real-world corroboration: widely deployed plugins (sqflite and similar) reply from their own background threads without crashing. On top of that, the finding asserts that every Android video upload crashes the process — compose_bar.dart:771/864 -> media_upload.dart:264 uploadVideo -> :276 _transcodeVideoToMp4 -> :742-745 invokeMethod -> MainActivity.kt:216 Thread{} -> :263 result.success is indeed the shipped path, so a hard crash there would mean the feature is 100% broken on Android in a released app, which is not credible without a repro. No crash, no security impact; at most a style nit about not hopping to the main thread.

Every later `submit_event` and `query_relay` resolves through `relay_api_base_url_with_override` (relay.rs:50-55) to the attacker's host, so all subsequent events signed with the user's real key — and every NIP-98 Authorization header built by `build_nip98_auth_header` (relay.rs:101-109) — are delivered to the attacker, and every read the app performs returns attacker-chosen events. Alternatively, passing an attacker-generated `nsec` replaces the live signing identity in memory: subsequent user actions are signed by a key the attacker holds while `get_identity` reports the substituted pubkey as if it were the user's own, and `create_ncryptsec_backup` would encrypt and hand back the substituted key. The frontend sends `before = last.created_at`; the relay's SQL becomes `created_at <= that_second ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20` and returns the identical 20 rows. Every subsequent 'Load more' returns the same page forever — the rest of the forum's history is unreachable, and the list visibly duplicates the boundary post even in the ordinary case.
